St. Sabbas the Sanctified

Saints

St. Sabbas the Sanctified

St. Sava the Sanctified · Savva · St. Sabas of Palestine

Period
Fifth–sixth century;532 in the OCA’s received life
Region
Cappadocia; Jerusalem; Judaean desert
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Abbot
Commemoration
December 5

Introduction

St. Sabbas is remembered as a Cappadocian monk and founder of Palestinian monastic communities. The OCA follows his formation under Theoktistos and Euthymios, settlement in the desert and the gathering of disciples around the Lavra.

Background

Sabas, (6), St., abbat in Palestine and founder of the laura of St. Sabas; born in 439, near Caesarea in Cappadocia. When 8 years old he entered a neighbouring monastery, and at 18 went a pilgrimage to the holy places at Jerusalem, where he entered the monastery of St. Passarion. At 30 he established himself as an anchorite in a cavern in the desert. Several persons joining him, he laid the foundations of his monastery on a rock on the Kidron river, where it still remains. (Cf. Murray's Handbook for Syria, p. 229.) …

Historical1911 dictionary article. Its dates are retained as that author’s chronology; the OCA gives532 for the repose. One sentence has been omitted rather than reproducing the dictionary’s erroneous identification of Sallustius’s patriarchal see; the omissions are visibly marked.

Life and notable events

… Several Armenians united themselves soon after to this community, which led to Sabas ordaining that the first part of Holy Communion should be said in Armenian, but the actual words of consecration in Greek. In 493 the monastery had increased so much that he built another at a short distance. He was sent as an ambassador to Constantinople in a.d. 511, by the patriarch ELIAS, to counteract the influence of Severus and the Monophysites with the emperor Anastasius; and again by Peter, patriarch of Jerusalem, in 531, to ask from the emperor remission of the taxes due by Palestine and help to rebuild the churches ruined by invasion. He died Dec. 5, 531, aged 91 years. …

[2] Historical reference or published author’s writing · Article Sabas,community and imperial missions

S. Euthymius chose him as his companion in his yearly retreats into the desert of Ruban. In one of these wanderings in the wilderness, Sabas discovered a cavern in the face of a precipice that overhung the brook Cedron. He reached it with some difficulty, and then hung a cord from the mouth, by which he was enabled to ascend to it and descend from it. He was aged forty when he retired to the cavern, and by the end of five years he saw himself surrounded by seventy disciples, whom he lodged in caves near him. He had much difficulty, however, in obtaining a supply of water, as that of Cedron was not drinkable; but one moonlight night he saw a wild ass pawing the gravelly soil at a distance from the brook, and, when it had made a hole, drinking the water that filtered through the gravel and sand into the place. This was a hint to Sabas, and he opened a well at the spot, and found a sufficiency of potable water. …

A passage from Baring-Gould’s1914 historical retelling. Its reconstruction of the early settlement is attributed to that author; its date language and explanations are not a new monastic rule.

[3] Historical reference or published author’s writing · VolXV,December5,printedp54,desert settlement and water

Death and martyrdom

The OCA records his repose in532 after a long monastic life, with no martyrdom described. Its date differs from the531 printed in the historical dictionary excerpt, and the two chronologies remain attributed.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Closing life

Writings and legacy

The received life associates St. Sabbas with the Jerusalem Typikon and with the growth of Palestinian monasteries. It recounts foundations, aid during drought and healing stories as part of his commemorative tradition, rather than a new rule composed by this app.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Foundations and Jerusalem Typikon
